code.title: Virtual DOM: diff two trees into minimal patches

followUps:
No. The virtual DOM is extra work on top of the real DOM, so a hand-tuned direct update of one known node is usually faster.

React's value is that it finds the changes for you. Updating one text node by hand costs 1 write; React renders the component, diffs the tree and then does that same 1 write. The win is correctness and maintainability when many parts of the UI depend on state.

They skip the virtual tree and compile templates so each piece of state is wired straight to the DOM node that uses it.

In Svelte a compiler turns count += 1 into code that sets one text node. In Solid, fine-grained signals re-run only the expressions that read the changed value. So an update touches O(places that use the value) instead of re-running a component and diffing its whole tree. The trade-off is a compile step and different rules about reactivity.

code.title: Reconciliation: same type keeps state, new type remounts

followUps:
The old element and everything below it is destroyed, including all its state, and a brand new one is created.

Example: a <div> holding a counter at 5 is replaced by a <section> at the same position. Effects clean up, the DOM node is removed, and the new section mounts with the counter back at 0. The same happens if a component function changes from A to B, even if they look alike.

React does not detect moves across parents, so a moved subtree is unmounted at the old place and mounted fresh at the new one, losing state.

Also, without keys, inserting an item at the front of a 1000-item list makes React compare every position and update all of them. Define components outside other components too: a component created inside render is a new type each time and remounts on every render. Keys fix reordering among siblings, not moves between parents.

code.title: Keys: index keys attach state to the wrong row

followUps:
Change the key. A different key means a different identity, so React throws away the old instance and mounts a new one with fresh state.

Example: <Profile key={userId} />. When userId goes from 7 to 8, the form inside starts empty instead of showing the previous user's half typed text. It is a clean alternative to resetting state in an effect.

React warns, and the behaviour becomes unreliable because two siblings claim the same identity.

With keys [a, b, a] and one a removed, React cannot tell which one went, so it may drop the wrong row, keep stale state, or duplicate/omit children on updates. Fix it by using a truly unique ID from the data, for example the database primary key, not a name that can repeat.

code.title: Fiber: interruptible work loop with shouldYield

followUps:
To catch impure code. In development React runs your render twice and compares, so side effects hidden inside render show up as odd or doubled results.

Since the render phase may be paused, restarted or thrown away, it must give the same output for the same input. StrictMode also mounts, unmounts and remounts effects once to check cleanup. A render that pushes to an outside array adds 2 items per render in development, which reveals the bug. Production renders once.

Because React does not store hook names; it stores them as a list and matches them by position.

On render 1, useState is call #0 and useEffect is call #1. If a condition skips the first call on render 2, the effect would read slot 0 and receive the state. So never call hooks in if, loops or after early returns; put the condition inside the hook instead.

The current tree is what is on screen now; the work-in-progress tree is the draft React builds for the next update.

Each fiber has an alternate pointing to its twin. React edits the draft, which can be paused or discarded without the user seeing anything. At commit it just flips root.current to the draft, and the old tree becomes the spare for the next render. This is double buffering, like drawing the next video frame off-screen.

code.title: Automatic batching: three setState calls, one render

followUps:
Because state is a snapshot: the variable count is a constant for that render, and setCount only asks for a later render.

If count is 0, then setCount(count + 1); console.log(count); prints 0. The new value 1 shows up as the count of the next render. If you need the next value now, compute it into a local variable first: const next = count + 1;.

Yes, when the updates are separated by an await or a separate tick, or when you force a flush.

Example: setA(1); await fetch(u); setB(2); gives 2 renders, because the await splits the work into two ticks. Updates with different priorities, like a click update and a transition update, can also render separately. Calling flushSync between two setters gives 2 renders as well.

flushSync forces React to render and commit the update immediately and synchronously, instead of waiting to batch it.

A normal update waits until the callback ends, so reading the DOM right after the setter shows old content. After flushSync(() => setItems(next)) the DOM already has the new rows, so you can scroll to the last one. It costs an extra render and hurts performance, so use it rarely.

Tearing is when different parts of the screen show different values of the same external store in one render, because the store changed while React was paused.

Example: a store changes from 1 to 2 mid-render, so a header shows 1 and a footer shows 2. useSyncExternalStore reads a snapshot and, if the store changed during rendering, redoes that render synchronously so all components see the same value. Always return a cached snapshot, or it loops.

No. A transition does the same work, or more, but spreads it out and puts it behind urgent updates.

If filtering 10,000 rows costs 200 ms, a transition still costs 200 ms of CPU (or more if it restarts), but typing stays smooth because it can be interrupted every few ms. It improves responsiveness, not throughput. To cut the work itself, virtualize the list or memoize.

React throws away the half finished transition render and starts again with the newest value.

The typing update is urgent, so it renders first and the input stays responsive. The old transition would show stale data, so it is abandoned, never committed. Example: you type 'a', 'ab', 'abc' quickly; only the render for 'abc' gets committed. Because renders can be abandoned, they must be pure.

code.title: Debounce vs transition: when work actually runs

followUps:
Because the value must update instantly on every keystroke, and transition updates are low priority and can lag behind.

If the input value is set inside startTransition, a keystroke may render late, so the text jumps or a typed character seems lost. Keep setQuery(e.target.value) urgent, and put only the expensive derived part, like the filtered list, in the transition or in a deferred value.

isPending is true while the transition render is still being prepared, so you know the screen is showing old content.

Use it to dim the list, show a small spinner, or disable a button, for example style={{opacity: isPending ? 0.5 : 1}}. It switches back to false when the new UI commits. It lets you give feedback without replacing the old content with a blank fallback.

Because a new promise each render is a new pending operation, so React would suspend forever, never reaching a resolved one.

If you write use(fetch(url)) in render, every retry creates another request, which becomes pending again, an endless loop. Create the promise in a parent, a cache, a Server Component or a framework loader, and pass it down so retries reuse the same promise and read its result.

Give each widget its own Suspense boundary so the fast one is not held back by the slow one.

Example: <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton/>}><Revenue/></Suspense> for a 100 ms widget and another boundary for a 3 s report. Revenue shows at 100 ms; the report shows a skeleton until 3 s. One big boundary at the top would show nothing for 3 s. Do not make it too fine, or the page flickers with many spinners.

It is a short minimum time (about 300 ms in React) that React waits before swapping in a new fallback or revealing content, so the screen does not flash.

If data arrives after 20 ms, showing a spinner and then content immediately looks like a flicker. React holds back briefly, so UI changes in one calmer step. It is an internal heuristic and you usually do not configure it.

Props must be serializable: plain data, not functions or class instances.

Strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, plain objects, Dates, Maps, Sets and promises can cross. An onClick function cannot, because the client cannot get server code. Functions marked with 'use server' (Server Actions) are the exception: they pass as references. Also never pass secrets, since everything in props goes to the browser.

Pass the server component as children or another prop from a parent that is a Server Component.

For example <Modal><ServerCart/></Modal> where Modal is a client component. The server renders ServerCart first and passes the result as a slot. What you cannot do is import a server component inside a client file, since that would turn it into a client component.

A Server Action is a function that runs on the server and that a client can call, usually from a form or button.

It is a public HTTP endpoint, so treat it like an API route: check that the user is signed in, check they may do this action on this record, validate every input (for example with a schema), and protect against CSRF and double submits. Never trust IDs sent from the browser, such as a hidden userId field.

Put it as low (as close to the leaves) as possible, because everything imported by a client file joins the client bundle.

If you mark a whole page 'use client' to make one button work, the page and its imported libraries ship to every visitor. Instead, make just a small <LikeButton/> a client component and keep the rest on the server. That keeps JS small, for example 5 KB for the button instead of 200 KB for the page.

Mostly TTFB and LCP differ, because they depend on where and when the HTML is built; INP depends mainly on JavaScript after load.

SSG/ISR from a CDN: lowest TTFB (tens of ms) and good LCP. SSR: higher TTFB, since the server works before sending. CSR: fast TTFB but poor LCP, because content waits for JS and data. INP is about main-thread work: a CSR or heavily hydrated page often has worse INP than a mostly static one.

Use on-demand revalidation: when the price changes, your backend calls an endpoint that tells the framework to regenerate that page now.

In Next.js this is revalidatePath('/product/42') or revalidateTag('product-42'). The next visitor gets fresh HTML, instead of waiting for the timer. Time based revalidate of 60 s is the fallback, so the price is at most 60 s old.

Because ISR HTML is cached and shared by everyone, so any user specific content in it is served to the next visitor.

If the page reads a cookie and prints 'Hello Ann' and that output is cached, Bob can receive 'Hello Ann'. Keep cached pages free of per-user data and fetch it on the client or in a dynamic part. Also be careful with CDN cache keys and cookies.

code.title: Hydration mismatch: server HTML vs first client render

followUps:
No. React 17 and later attach listeners once at the root container and use event delegation, not one per element.

Hydration only links existing DOM nodes to fibers and records handlers as props. A click is caught at the root and routed to the right fiber. So 5,000 buttons do not mean 5,000 listeners, which saves memory and hydration time.

The hydration gap is the time between the page looking ready (HTML shown) and being interactive (JS downloaded and hydrated); clicks in it can be ignored or delayed.

Reduce it by sending less JS (Server Components, code splitting), using Suspense for selective hydration so clicked parts hydrate first, and loading below-the-fold widgets lazily. For example, cutting 400 KB of JS can reduce hydration from 600 ms to 250 ms on a mid-range phone.

It is React 18's ability to hydrate Suspense boundaries independently and in priority order, instead of the whole page at once.

Each boundary hydrates when its code is ready, and if the user clicks inside a not yet hydrated boundary, React hydrates that one first and replays the click. A slow comments section no longer blocks the header and article from becoming interactive.

Collect real-user error reports from the browser and group them, because hydration errors only happen on real devices.

Use onRecoverableError in hydrateRoot to send the message and page URL to your logging tool, and check the production console text, which is minified so use the error code link. Look for patterns, such as one locale or timezone. Also test in staging with different time zones.

Lazy hydration speeds up the first load but leaves some parts not interactive for longer, and can delay content that crawlers or users expect to act on.

For SEO the HTML is already in the page, so crawlers see content either way. For users, a menu that only hydrates on interaction needs a short wait on the first click, which may be noticeable. Hydrate critical controls (menu, search) early and only defer below-the-fold or rarely used widgets.

When the page is highly interactive, because Server Components cannot hold state, run effects or react to browser events.

Editors, drawing tools, dashboards with live filtering, drag and drop, and maps need client components, and their JS has to hydrate. For those, split the code, hydrate on demand, move heavy work to a Web Worker, and keep the static surrounding content on the server.

A waterfall is when requests wait for each other one after another although they could run together, so total time is the sum of all of them.

Example: const user = await getUser(); const posts = await getPosts(); with 200 ms each gives 400 ms; Promise.all gives 200 ms. Spot it in the network or tracing view as stair steps, or by timing each await with logs. Nested components that each fetch can also create waterfalls.

Streaming lowers time to first byte but not total time: the server sends the shell at once and the slow parts later.

Without streaming, a page whose slowest query takes 2 s has TTFB of about 2 s. With streaming, the shell goes out at about 100 ms and the slow section arrives at 2 s. The user sees something sooner (better FCP and often LCP), while the whole page finishes at about the same time.

Partial Prerendering builds the static shell at build time and serves it from the CDN instantly, then streams the dynamic parts into holes on request.

Here the layout, header and shared content come from the edge in tens of milliseconds, and the slow personalised or fresh data component sits inside Suspense and streams in. You get fast TTFB without turning the whole page into slow SSR.
